subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONTRIBUTIONS OF FLOUR AND DRIED SKIM MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I should like to make an announcement respecting two important matters which are referred to in the supplementary estimates.
It will be recalled that when the heads of governments of the NATO countries met in Paris in December, 1957 I brought forward a proposal for the establishment of a food bank among the NATO countries for use particularly in the event of any outbreak of hostilities.	At that time I expressed the
willingness of the Canadian government to play its part in the establishment of such an institution. The house was made aware of the facts of this question on July 19 of last year, during the debate on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Since then and throughout the year discussions have been going forward in NATO, and directly with interested countries, to determine under what conditions a Canadian contribution to NATO food stockpiles in Europe might be made. These discussions were most useful, and I am hopeful that it will not be long before it will be feasible for a Canadian contribution to be made effective.
I would therefore advise the house that the government has now decided to ask 66968-9-266J
parliament to provide $10 million for the current year by an item in the supplementary estimates, such an amount to provide for Canadian flour for storage.
I would also, subject to the approval of parliament, like to say it has been decided to make available free of charge an additional 20 million pounds of dried skim milk to relief agencies, both national and international, for distribution to needy people in other parts of the world. While some of this milk will be used to meet emergency requirements, the bulk of it will be used to provide people, and particularly children, in the less developed countries with a supplementary source of food and a much needed means of balancing their diet.
Of the 30 million pounds which we set aside on the same basis for the use of relief agencies in the past year, nearly half has now been taken up by UNICEF, the Unitarian service committee of Canada, the Canadian Lutheran world relief agency, the Canadian council of churches and CARE of Canada. It is expected that the balance of the amount previously set aside, together with the additional supplies which are now being made available, will help these and similar organizations to carry on with the humanitarian work which they have been doing in other parts of the world.
These particular items are Nos. 506 and 510 respectively in the supplementary estimates.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONTRIBUTIONS OF FLOUR AND DRIED SKIM MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal for the establishment of a NATO food bank, which has been under consideration for some time, is one which certainly commends itself to those on this side of the house. This is one reason, Mr. Speaker, why we were somewhat discouraged a year or so ago-perhaps not as long back as that-when the United States state department representative indicated to the congressional committee that not much progress was being made in that direction. The Prime Minister has now announced that as far as Canada is concerned, a specific proposal has been made to set aside a certain amount-I think he said for flour-to initiate this NATO food bank.
If this food bank is to be successful it will have to be participated in by other NATO countries. I am not in a position now to express an opinion on whether the bank will

NATO Food Bank
be more effective through the storage of flour than wheat. It is one of the things that will have to be gone into, but the principle of a food bank seems to us to be a good one, and if it can be carried out on a NATO basis it will receive support from this side.
I have read, Mr. Speaker, that recently the United States, which should be participating, of course, in this kind of enterprise, has shown more interest in the President's food for peace proposal, about which there have been discussions I think in Washington or New York, I am not sure which, recently. It is to be hoped that these two ventures will not conflict.
So far as making available skim milk powder for relief is concerned, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture will recall that my colleague the hon. member for Essex East brought up this matter during the discussion of the minister's estimates, I think it was, and he received a rather discouraging reply from the minister in regard to his proposal. I have understood from what the minister and others have said that it has been difficult to find relief agencies and others who are interested in the amount of skim milk we have been able to make available to them, and I hope the announcement of the Prime Minister this afternoon indicates that that particular difficulty has been overcome. I cannot think of any better way to use surpluses of this kind than for the purposes indicated by the Prime Minister.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Minister of Finance make a statement on the important and novel financial operation announced by the government on Friday last? Perhaps in his statement he might also include an explanation as to why the announcement was not made in the House of Commons before it was given to the press.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday morning at 9 o'clock the wires, in the usual way, were delivered to those who are interested in financial offerings of this kind. The offering is an invitation in respect of up to $200 million of government of Canada one year treasury bills dated June 10 for sale through competitive
Inquiries of the Ministry tender. Payment for the treasury bills may be made in either cash or by exchange of government of Canada bonds of the issue which matures on July 1 next. Tenders will be received up to the closing hour of five o'clock on Tuesday, June 2, that is tomorrow, from primary distributors of new issues of government of Canada securities. The Minister of Finance reserves the right to accept or reject any tender in whole or in part.
This is the first time, Mr. Speaker, the government has issued or offered treasury bills of one year maturity. We have long been accustomed to bills of three months' maturity. Recently we have been offering bills with six months' maturity. The former government for several years had offered bills of a nine months' maturity. The one year maturity is a well established treasury bill in the experience of the United States.
As to the second part of the hon. gentleman's question, may I say that it has never been the practice to announce offerings of this kind in the house before they are made public. These offerings are regularly made whether of treasury bills or of bond offerings. The treasury bill tenders are invited every week. The tenders are received and opened at noon every Thursday. That has been the practice followed for a long time both with regard to the three months' treasury bills and also lately with the six months' treasury bills.
So far as bond offerings are concerned, it has not been the practice to announce these in the house. As a matter of fact, they could not be announced in the house at a good time because the house meets in the afternoon. It has been the practice of my predecessors, as well as the practice that has been observed since we came into office two years ago, that these offerings go to the primary distributors by telegram for delivery at their offices at the opening of business on the morning chosen.

maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: In view of the fact that the minister himself has said that this was an unprecedented offering, and in view of the fact that the information was given to the press, does the minister not think it would have been at least a courtesy to have given parliament this information at eleven o'clock on Friday morning?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext:
There was no discourtesy to the house. The information was available. If there had been any question by the hon. gentleman I would have been glad to deal with it then. As a matter of fact I rather expected that he would have had a

Inquiries of the Ministry question. Questions have been asked repeatedly in the house about treasury bills by hon. gentlemen opposite. Their interest in this matter has been very keen. But, Mr. Speaker, the practice has not been to announce these matters in the house. If the house wishes information week by week as to treasury bills or special information of this kind, the house will certainly be given the information. But this information was made public at the same time as the telegrams of offering reached the desks and offices of those to whom they were directed.

maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: In view of the fact that this was an unprecedented offering may I ask the minister a supplementary question with regard to it. Is it a fact that 2J per cent bonds maturing on July 1 will be redeemed at 101.25 per cent instead of 100 per cent if they are exchanged for the new issue? If that is the case, why was it necessary to offer this particular inducement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the basis upon which this valuation is placed on the bonds to be turned in is contained in the following sentence in the prospectus:
Where 21 per cent government of Canada bonds due July 1st are offered in exchange at a valuation of 101.25 per cent they must be in bearer form with the final coupon attached or if in registered form be accompanied by proper transfer documents.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has made quite a play on the use of the expression "unprecedented".

maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: You used it first.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: The thing that is unprecedented is simply the fact that the treasury bill has been given a 12 month maturity. I have already pointed out that we have had in this country three month, six month and nine month treasury bills. The form of the offering is new only in so far as this is a twelve month offering in place of some of those shorter maturities as in the past.

maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister whether he would explain to the house why unmatured victory bonds were called in last year, and now in effect one year treasury bills are being put in their place. Is the minister afraid of issuing a long term government bond?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. gentleman is just all mixed up. Last year what we offered was a conversion bond issue in return for victory bonds of five different maturities to the extent to

which the holders were prepared to exchange them. On this occasion, those who hold this bond which matures on July 1 next have the opportunity offered to them, if they agree to exercise it, to tender for these treasury bills up to the amount stated. It is entirely a matter for their own choice whether or not they tender for these bills, and it will remain a matter for choice on the part of the Minister of Finance to accept or refuse any tender in whole or in part.

maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: May I ask the minister why the government decided not to issue a long term government bond rather than proceed along these lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: We considered that in the public interest this was the best form of maturity to offer at this particular time for this particular amount.

maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: Is the minister aware that the highest United States short term treasury bill rate is 3 per cent, while our own exceeds 5 per cent, a differential of over 2 per cent?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext:
I think we have had a fairly
complete discussion of the question initiated by the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Welland has just asked a supplementary question which appears to be giving information rather than asking for it, and I suggest that we pass to the next topic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCE
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT TREASURY BILL ISSUE
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Speaker, a very misleading impression has been left by the observation which the hon. gentleman has just made, and I would ask the opportunity to set that right. Evidently the hon. member is not aware of the situation with respect to treasury bill rates in the United States. I happen to have them with me in a statement which reached my desk only today. On the 340 day bills in the United States the rate is 3.835 per cent average; on the 220 day bills it is 3.565 per cent average, and on the 1 year certificates, the 4 per cent coupon is offered on a 4.05 per cent basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
The first part of the question asks me whether this news dispatch is correct. Well, the news dispatch does bear a resemblance to the facts. The hon. gentleman may recall that the late lamented Gordon Graydon, in the days when he used to be one of the Canadian parliamentary observers at the United Nations, struck up quite a friendship, among many others with Mr. Gromyko. All those who knew Mr. Graydon will recall his affability. In conversation with Mr. Gromyko at the President's luncheon at the White House last Thursday I made some reference to the late Gordon Graydon, and Mr. Gromyko remembered very well the way in which Mr. Graydon used to exchange banter with him.
In those days the word "progressive" was the favourite word in the communist vocabulary, and Mr. Gromyko did not always differentiate very clearly between political parties which embraced the word "progressive" in their names. I did not say to him, though I might have, that there is one party in this house, namely the party to which the hon. gentleman belongs, which sometimes has a little difficulty with its name, too.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, May 29, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-49, to provide for the establishment of a national energy board-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 47-Revocation and suspension of certificate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: When the house rose on Friday last we were discussing clause 47 of the bill and the amendment proposed thereto by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the time the committee concluded the discussion last week I had moved, as you have indicated, an amendment to the effect that we omit from clause 47 the words "with the approval of the governor in council". I should like to remind the committee that clause 47 reads:
(1) Subject to subsection 2, the board may by order, with the approval of the governor in council, revoke or suspend a certificate-
-and so on. I would like to underline the word "may". When the minister replied to our amendment on the first occasion he indicated that there might be times and conditions under which a company that had received a certificate should not automatically be obligated to lose its licence or its certificate. He indicated that certain unforeseen conditions might arise. However, it is our submission that the bill as it reads enables the energy board to take such matters into consideration, in that the clause provides that the board may revoke or suspend a certificate once it is issued if the terms and conditions of the certificate are not, in the opinion of the board, being complied with. We feel that the word "may" is the important word and that the board would act in the national interest and would take all circumstances into adequate consideration. We do not see why the governor in council or government of the day should want to delegate unto itself the authority to police the implementation of the act.
I can remember well that a number of years ago we were considering in the house a pipe line company that had been issued a permit to build a trans-Canada natural gas pipe line. Time after time this particular pipe line company was unable or unwilling to meet the terms and conditions upon which it had


been granted its rights. I can remember the Conservatives, who were in opposition at the time, asking the government of the day to enforce the terms and conditions that had been imposed upon Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, but the government of the day procrastinated and continued to procrastinate. Six month extensions were granted one after another until many years elapsed from the time the pipe line was to have been built until it actually was built.
The Conservatives in the house at that *time expressed the opinion that the government of the day ought not to extend indefinitely the rights obtained by this pipe line company, and that if the company was unable to meet the terms and conditions which it had agreed to meet it should move out of the way and allow the formation of another pipe line company which would meet the needs of the Canadian nation in this regard. But here we have the Conservatives in office and asking that they be granted in this bill the same rights that were being exercised at that time by Right Hon. C. D. Howe. They are asking that we deny the energy board the right of enforcement of the terms and conditions attached to certificates. We find that the cabinet wants to retain this authority for itself.
We feel that once the energy board has recommended the issuance of a certificate and has set the terms and conditions the company must meet, once these terms and conditions have been reviewed by the cabinet and approved, thereafter the energy board, having issued a certificate either to build a pipe line or an international power line, should have the right to police the terms and conditions. In other words we believe that political considerations should not be a factor with regard to whether or not a company will be allowed to retain its certificate indefinitely irrespective of whether it obeys or flagrantly violates the terms and conditions to which it agrees. We cannot understand why the cabinet wants the authority to police the implementation of the conditions attached to the issuance of the certificate.
I remember quite well that on another occasion several years ago the house had under consideration the extension of the powers of the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act. In my opinion one of the strongest arguments put forward by the Conservatives, then in opposition, against the extension of the Emergency Powers Act was, as one of their members said at that time, that this would allow the government to aid and abet any corporation politically friendly to the government in office, and would also enable the cabinet to extinguish completely

a Canadian corporation that did not subscribe to the particular political aspirations of the government in office. That was when the Conservatives really put on a fight in the house. That was the beginning of the road into office for the Conservative party.
Yet now that they are in office they are in effect, in expressing their non-approval of the amendment, asking for the very same authority, the authority to reward their friends and punish their enemies, an authority which in years gone by they regretted was being held by the Liberal government of the day. We contend that once the rules of the game have been established by the energy board and approved by the government of the day the board should be allowed to be the referee. We should give the energy board the authority to enforce, wherever they may deem it advisable, the terms and conditions of the certificate.
Amendment (Mr. Regier) negatived: Yeas, 4; nays, 58.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Shall clause 47 carry?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. In explaining this clause on Friday last the minister indicated that it was modelled on section 3 of the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act, and left the matter there. On checking that section I notice that a substantial change seems to have been made in the bill now before the committee. I wonder if the minister would explain why the change was made, and the purpose of the change.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what is the substantial change to which the hon. member is referring and about which he wishes an explanation?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The former legislation provided an opportunity for any person licensed and in business, if he was not complying with any term or condition, to be given notice to bring himself into compliance with the term or condition. Under those circumstances the licence could not be revoked. Now a person has no protection; the new legislation gives him no protection at all.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I fail to understand that. Does not subclause 2 cover everything the hon. member has in mind? It reads:
No order shall be made under this section unless notice has been given to the holder of the certificate who is alleged to have violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof and an opportunity has been afforded to him of being heard.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better explain more fully the point I have in mind. The clause before the committee now reads in this way, clause 47 (1):
National Energy Board
Subject to subsection (2), the board may by order, with the approval of the governor in council revoke or suspend a certificate if, in the opinion of the board, the person to whom it was issued has violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof.
(2) No order shall be made under this section unless notice has been given to the holder of the certificate who is alleged to have violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof and an opportunity has been afforded to him of being heard.
It will be noted that if there is an allegation of failure to comply with a term there is an opportunity of being heard; but the board, after the hearing, may still revoke the licence. The relevant part of section 3 of the exportation of power and fluids act provides, as follows:
A licence granted under this section may be revoked if the governor in council is satisfied that
(a)	the licensee has refused or neglected to comply with any of the terms or conditions of the licence-[DOT]
That is practically the same in its meaning.
(b)	notice of such refusal or neglect has been sent to the licensee, and
(c)	the licensee has, after receiving such notice, refused or neglected to comply with any such terms or condition.
The point is that under that legislation the licensee had an opportunity of bringing himself into full compliance with the terms and conditions. Under the legislation now before the committee the licensee may neglect or fail to comply with some term or condition, and it is quite true he is given notice, but the board still has the power to revoke his licence even though the licensee has brought himself into full compliance with the terms and conditions. What I fear in that is that we are putting these licensees in a position of uncertainty that is not going to be helpful to all concerned. I would fear, looking at the clause, that it is something more than was intended when the legislation was being considered.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think it was intended to be more stringent than the provision in the exportation of power and fluids act. I see the hon. member's point, that the wording in that act permits the licensee to restore his position. We thought the fact that there was a hearing, or an opportunity to state his position, would obviously lead him to restore himself to the position in which he was before if he inadvertently failed to comply with some of the terms or conditions.
In any event there is a further protection, is there not, in that if the board errs in making an order after the licensee has complied with the conditions, the governor in council has a chance to review that decision because the approval of the governor in council is required. May I assure my hon. friend that

National Energy Board there was no intention of making it more stringent than the old clause. I feel that the new wording is not overly severe and that the licensee, because of the public hearing, will have a chance to get his position understood by the board.
There was not a hearing in the exportation of power and fluids act. There was first the alleged refusal or neglect to comply with conditions, then the notice, and then the order if the licensee refused or neglected to comply with the terms or conditions. The hearing provides him with an opportunity to appear and state his case, and this opportunity was not granted to him under the other legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am afraid it is not quite as simple as that. It is reasonable to assume that there will be terms and conditions to a great many of these licences, some of them of a fairly technical nature but not, in themselves, of major importance. We are being asked in the present bill to give the power of revocation of a licence because of neglect to comply with one of such terms or conditions, an absolute power of revocation. I am suggesting to the minister that this provision is much more severe than the facts warrant in such cases, and that the effect will be to leave a cloud hanging over these licences that may do the very thing the minister desires not to do.
He spoke, at several earlier stages of this bill, of the necessity for large investment in these operations. It is clauses such as this one that make the obtaining of such investment needlessly difficult. What we want to be sure of here is a proper hearing and proper protection when licences are granted, and once they are granted we do not want to give a right to revoke a licence needlessly. I feel this is the real point, and I believe it is something that should be investigated because of the fears I have mentioned.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I certainly appreciate the hon. member's views on this matter. He quite approves of the review by the governor in council or the approval of the governor in council being required before orders such as these are made. I believe there is sufficient protection because of that opportunity for the person to be heard. The board would hold a hearing and then make its findings after a full discussion of all the facts involved. This is like clause 44, in which the approval of the governor in council is required.
The seriousness of the whole situation I pointed out, myself, when we were debating this on Friday. We appreciated that in both instances, in the granting of the certificate and second in a case where it had to be

revoked. We were relying on a public hearing in both instances, and then an actual act by the board by way of an order which finally had to come to the governor in council for approval. I think in both instances there is sufficient protection.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There is one small point that perhaps I should clarify first. I do not want my remarks on this section to necessarily indicate approval of the governor in council. I merely took the position that as the minister will recall, having granted that power in clause 44 it seems to me that it is necessary to grant it here. I do not want to raise or reopen that matter.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I realize the situation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think I had better bring the matter to a head. I think there should be an amendment to this clause. 1 therefore move:
That section 47 of Bill C-49 be replaced by the following:
"A certificate may be revoked or suspended by the board, with the approval of the governor in council, if the board is satisfied that:
(a)	the holder of the certificate has refused or neglected to comply with any of the terms and conditions of the certificate;
(b)	notice of such refusal or neglect has been sent to such holder; and
(c)	the holder has, after receiving such notice, refused or neglected to comply with any such term or condition."
Perhaps I do not need to elaborate on it.

The regulation could be of such a kind, as the hon. member for Ottawa West has said, as to be prohibitive or to be impossible of performance. At the moment I cannot think what such a regulation would be, but it is conceivable that if the governor in council, for some reason or another, wished to avoid the continuance of benefit of a particular holder of a certificate, the governor in council might well pass a regulation which could not possibly be met by the owner of the certificate at the time. National Energy Board fully. Then of course my hon. friend recognizes the fact that acts are sometimes subject to alteration in subsequent sessions. This clause ensures that, despite changes of that nature in the act or in the regulations, the holders of certificates are expected to comply.

speechtext: Ye gods.

speechtext: This amendment does not remove my desire to ask a question on this clause. Clause 49 is modelled on section 37 of the Pipe Lines Act. There is

National Energy Board no change in that wording. The limit to the length of the line which may be exempted is still 25 miles, just as it reads in the Pipe Lines act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: But this limit may now be raised in any specific case if the approval of the governor in council is obtained.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is the very point. Under the original wording the board is absolutely supreme up to 25 miles. There is an amendment now being suggested, and I think I agree with the amendment as far as it goes, but it does not go far enough because there are still left in the words "or such other length as the governor in council may prescribe." I personally have no criticism of the fact that the board might have the power to make exemptions in certain circumstances when the line does not exceed 25 miles in length, but I cannot understand why the governor in council should be given authority to make exemptions covering lines longer than 25 miles. The lines subject to such exemptions could go right across Canada. Under this clause as it reads at present there is actually authority to construct a second trans-Canada pipe line, exempted from all the regulations and rules of this entire bill at the whim and purpose of the governor in council.
Surely if this act means anything at all, regulations, once they have been made, should be enforced. Surely the exemptions from the provisions of this bill of lines up to 25 miles is sufficient. When I said "ye Gods" a few moments ago I was referring to some of the acts which are already on the statute book and to what the hon. member has just said about the power of the executive cabinet. As long as these words "or such other length as the governor in council may prescribe" are left in the bill complete authority is given to the governor in council to wipe out this entire bill together with all its regulations and provisions, setting aside all questions of financial conditions, locations and operation across the length and breadth of Canada. That is exactly what these words mean.
I do not know just how to proceed, now that the leader of the house has moved an amendment, but I certainly wish to suggest an additional amendment to the effect that subclause 1 of clause 49 be amended by deleting the words "or such other length as the governor in council may prescribe".

speechtext: Order.

speechtext: Before a decision is taken on the amendment which the leader of the house has proposed, may I say that I intend to move an amendment which deals particularly with the points which have been brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver East. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

speechtext:
May I say that I am in entire agreement with my hon. friend. Had the government taken another course I was ready to intervene at some length. I can recall, in one case which came before the courts, a defendent using a minister's interpretation of a bill in an effort to show what the legislation was intended to do, and the judge telling him that it was not what the minister said in the house or anything else that mattered when it came to interpretation, it was simply the wording of the act.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clause 50 agreed to.
On clause 51-Tolls to be approved.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while the vote on our last amendment was being taken I distinctly heard the tall and elongated hon. member for Halifax refer to this group as dedicated dough heads. I think that is getting marginal as far as parliamentary language is concerned. My colleagues remind me that a speech made by one of the so called dedicated dough heads prior to my rising influenced the Minister of Public Works to rise and move an amendment along the lines he suggested. I do not think, therefore, it is fair to refer to this small but hard working group as dedicated dough heads.
It is not my habit to indulge in unparliamentary language but when I look at the hon. member he reminds me of my asparagus patch and of the fact that the higher you go up an asparagus stalk the softer and less useful it becomes.
We take strong exception to clause 51 because it differs entirely from the recommendations of the royal commission on energy. I want to place on the record a few of those recommendations and a paragraph commenting upon them. The commissioners dealt at considerable length with this problem. At page 27 of the report we find recommendations in this respect as follows:
The commission recommends:
1. That the Pipe Lines Act, R.S.C., 1952, Chapter 211, be amended to provide that:
That, of course, refers to the Pipe Lines Act as it then stood. I continue:
(a)	It shall be mandatory for the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to exercise the powers conferred upon it under part II of the Pipe Lines Act, with respect to the regulation of the traffic, tolls or tariffs of oil pipe-line companies subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
(b)	It should not be a condition precedent to the exercise of such powers that an oil pipe-line company be declared to be a "common carrier";
(c)	It shall be mandatory for the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to regulate
National Energy Board the prices of rates of gas pipe-line companies subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and, in so doing, to require, if necessary, any such gas pipe-line company to renegotiate the terms of any existing contracts for the sale or delivery of gas for distribution or consumption within Canada;
(d)	It shall be mandatory for the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada periodically, and at least once in every 24-month period during the early years of regulation, to review and, if deemed necessary, to adjust the prices, tolls, rates and tariffs of pipe-line companies regulated by it;
At the conclusion of the recommendations the report states:
That the prices, tolls, rates or tariffs of a company owning or operating an oil or gas pipe line, as regulated by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, should be just and reasonable, non-discriminatory and calculated to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity, after making due allowance for reasonable and proper operating expenses, depreciation, interest, income and other taxes.
We agree with that recommendation. In commenting on the recommendations, the commissioners say:
Although the Pipe Lines Act gives the board of transport commissioners the authority to regulate the traffic, tolls or tariffs of oil pipe lines, subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, this authority has not been exercised, although the board did conduct a formal hearing on a complaint raised by a shipper of crude oil. No regulatory body of the government of Canada has the authority at the present time to regulate the selling prices or transportation charges of gas pipe lines subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. The commission considers that a more positive and active approach to the question of regulation has now become necessary.
The members in this group agree 100 per cent with that opinion of the royal commission. I go now to another paragraph in the commentary:
In view of the great need of the Canadian economy for supplies of heat and energy producing fuels, it is desirable to ensure not only that adequate supplies are available at all times, but also that prices are kept at a reasonable level. As crude oil and natural gas must be moved over long distances to reach the principal market areas of Canada, transportation charges must be no more than are fair and reasonable. The commission is of the view that the board of transport commissioners should have all the powers needed for the regulation of the prices or rates, traffic, tolls or tariffs or pipe-line companies subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
We believe those are very wise recommendations and comments. We believe it is very necessary that the national energy board have the same responsibilities in this respect as the public utilities commissions in the provinces. In British Columbia power companies, provincial transportation companies such as bus and trucking firms, public carriers and telephone companies, go before the public utilities commission in order to have their rates established by that body. That has been found an excellent practice since it began. It is not

National Energy Board a question of those companies establishing rates and then going into operation and the commission reviewing them after some period, but before they are established they must be set on the basis of an order from the public utilities commission.
We believe for the protection of the interests of industry and of the Canadian people generally the same practice and procedure should be followed in this bill and that we should accept the recommendations of the royal commission in this respect. I therefore move seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East:
That section 51 be amended by inserting the words "and approved by" alter the words "filed with".

I would draw attention to clause 53-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: We did not have in mind that it was an automatic approval by any means because, as I had intended to point out, clause 53 gives the board the power to disallow after it has had a chance to review the tariff. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that clause 50, which we have passed, gives the board power to make orders with respect to tolls, that is, to levy tolls? maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I believe the rule is that one cannot refer to proceedings in a committee of the house, but in one of the committees of the house this year we have had a number of meetings in which there were a number of questions asked about the rates of the air transport board. Once a rate is filed and accepted by that board it remains a tariff and is unchanged; but there is nothing here that makes it clear that a tariff which is filed has to be accepted. The evidence before the committee dealing with the air transport board tariff situation was that the tariff could be challenged; it could be changed; it could be amended. This also has some connection with the minister's own statement when he referred to the profits which could be made or which such pipe lines would be allowed to make.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: On clause 18.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: It was a different point. It had to do with a question of law or jurisdiction.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That was on clause 18, but certain people went on to discuss other matters, and the question of an appeal on fact was also under consideration, and an explanation of that was made. We looked at it in this way. There has to be some element of finality somewhere and with a board of competent and experienced people examining all the facts that they would have to examine prior to determining whether tolls are just and reasonable, it would be undesirable for that fact finding activity of the board to be placed under review through an appeal. With the provision of an appeal on law and jurisdiction we thought that the rights of Canadians were adequately protected; but this is a specialized operation, determining from a mass of figures and calculations what constitutes a just and reasonable toll, and we were placing this responsibility on the board to make that decision. If, for example, an appeal on fact were carried, as it is in some other matters, to the governor in council, we would be in a difficult position in having to review all matters pertaining to what is admittedly a complicated problem, and we would not be in the same position as the board itself as it gathers experience on this subject. Therefore, it was for these reasons we decided that we should give this a trial, anyway. We are not making claim to any superior intelligence in drafting clauses of this bill. This is our best judgment at the moment. If in the course of time we find that this is not the most satisfactory method of dealing with the matter we shall have to
National Energy Board take a second look at it, but for the moment we think the board should be given the opportunity of gaining experience, sizing up the problem, and as time elapses advising us as to whether or not this is the best way in which this difficult subject should be considered. This is another reason why we have placed it as we have and have said that there shall be no appeal from its finding of fact.

speechtext: That is right.

speechtext: -and I am afraid-and this applies to many of us-words uttered are not always monuments of clarity. His certainly were not clear on that point. speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I think we have to go a little farther than that. The first report of the royal commission on energy, the Borden commission report, went a very great length in its recommendations dealing with the regulation of pipe line companies and on this particular point a recommendation was made that tolls, in addition to other requirements, be calculated to yield a fair return on the shareholders' equity and so on. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I always listen with attention to my hon. friend who has been looking at this bill with care but I doubt very much if we need to go into a lengthy debate with regard to what was intended and meant by the Borden commission and what was intended by somebody else's remarks. In this particular instance clause 52 is identical with section 42 of the Pipe Lines Act. Here again we are leaving the matter to the board, rather than setting out some rigid, specific formula, so that the board may determine what is just and reasonable. We weighed very carefully the submission in the Borden report and gave it full consideration. But again we decided that for flexibility it would be wise to let the board work this out, determine how these tolls shall be applied, what is a just and reasonable toll and how it shall be related to the company's operations.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I can clarify it. I do not want to delay the thing unduly but

it seemed to me that in part of recommendation No. 12 the Borden commission went quite too far and made a recommendation that was defective, to use a very mild word to describe it. I am glad to see that the minister has recognized that the legislation in force on this point, put there by the former government, did assert proper principles and that those principles are the ones that are being carried forward in this bill. I found myself in some difficulty with respect to the minister's and the Prime Minister's remarks because the impression seemed to be capable of being drawn from the two sets of remarks, together with the Borden commission report, that a change was being made in the clause as to tolls now being adopted and it is not. It is not changed at all. I think that clarifies the matter a good deal. I do not like making general remarks about the minister's statement on the earlier stage of the bill but his remarks and the Prime Minister's on this point were certainly of a nature, when read together with the Borden commission report, as to create a very bad misunderstanding on this subject and really were capable of misleading those who were not careful in trying to understand the subject and who did not read the remarks carefully.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that a reading of the Prime Minister's statement on May 26 cannot but give the impression that the alleged weaknesses of the previous legislation on the subject with respect to the protection of the public interest were to be removed by this particular bill. The Prime Minister stated, as found on page 4021 of Hansard:
Finally there is the question of whether the public interest will be protected.
Then he went on to show how this bill would be more effective in that regard than the previous legislation. Also, on page 4025 the Prime Minister said:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interest. With the implementation of this legislation, no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their energy than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy.
Presumably this is the clause of the bill under which that is to be guaranteed, so I should like the minister to tell us how this particular clause, which lays down the general criterion of equity and reasonableness, is to be more effective in the protection of the public interest, the prevention of unnecessary profiteering and all that kind of thing than the previous legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is hoped that the board, through its careful consideration of all these problems, will end up with formulae which will be just and reasonable and that the interests of Canadian consumers will be protected. I feel that, from the experience of the past, that will be very much in the minds of the board. It is difficult to spell out things like that in legislation but a board, with all the facts before it, and with the public interest in mind, will be able to determine for us, in the Canadian interest, what is just and reasonable. We have deliberately left this flexible so that the board will have room to manoeuvre and come to conclusions in an area of business, and business regulation, which is new to Canada.
We have noticed the experience of the people across the line with regard to this and we gather from observation that some flexibility would be very much worth while. Starting off as we are here, with the intention to bring together the various methods that have been used in the past with regard to the oil and gas industry and with regard to electric power, we feel this is the best way to make a start by allowing the board, in its wisdom, to determine what is just and reasonable. We thought it was better that flexibility should be permitted rather than spelling out the specific means right in the bill.
If my hon. friend finds, as time passes by, that the national interest has suffered or that Canadians have been discriminated against, I am sure he will be amongst the first to rise and point out this fact to us. I hope he will do so. However, I feel that we have a great chance here of having the Canadian interest protected by giving the board this freedom of action.

speechtext:

I have no quarrel with the statement as such, but I have a quarrel with the relationship of the statement to the very inflexible words of the Prime Minister to the effect that the price to be charged for gas and power must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interest. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There is a further explanation which the minister may give when he comes back. This clause provides that where the gas transmitted by a company through its pipe line from any place within a province to any place outside the province is the property of the company, the board can fix a proportion of the difference between the amount paid by the company for the gas and the amount for which the gas is sold. But there is no such provision in the case of oil.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let us look at the terms of the clause. The wording reads:
Where the gas transmitted by a company through its pipe line from any place within a province to any place outside the province is the property of the company-
Here we have a situation where a company owns the pipe line. It buys the gas in one province and sells it to another end in

National Energy Board another province, but it owns the pipe line in which the gas is being transmitted. That,
I can understand. But what is the meaning of what follows?
-such proportion as the board may fix of the differential between the amount paid by the company for the gas and the amount for which the gas is sold by the company shall for the purposes of this Part be deemed to be a toll charged by the company to the purchaser for the transmission thereof.
What in the name of heaven does that mean?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This clause 61 has no
counterpart in existing energy legislation. Recommendation 11 subsection (c) of the Borden report has been questioned on the ground that parliament had no power in peace time to control the prices charged for gas by transmission companies. The provinces, of course, claim jurisdiction over the price of gas at the point of origin and at the point of consumption. The price jurisdiction which the government would exercise is that on prices charged by interprovincial companies transmitting gas to their customers, that is, to the companies which buy gas for resale either to other gas companies or to consumers. While these prices cannot legally be controlled, the actual transmission charges of the pipe line company can, since they are similar to the freight rates on railroads. In the case of gas pipe lines the commodity carried is generally the property of the carrier and no transmission charge as such is levied. It is, however, provided here that in such case a proportion of the difference between the price paid for the gas and the price at which it is sold by the transmission company shall be deemed to be a toll.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Is it not simply a matter of the provinces having jurisdiction over the purchase price and the sale price of the gas and an attempt by this government to put forward something which would prevent exorbitant differentials? This is only a partial protection of the public in the sense that the companies can pay any price they wish for their product, or sell it at any price they wish but that the differential, which is the only element which this parliament can control, may be subjected to a limiting toll. The clause could very well have been put in in the early part of the bill as a definition of the word "toll". That is where it should have been included. This is the only way in which the board can control the price paid by consumers in the event of an abnormal transmission charge being made. I am not suggesting that this would happen, because I am sure that no producer would want to do any such thing. But the problem is still there.

It still remains, and this clause does not really take care of it. However, it goes about as far as we can go constitutionally.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister if this is not precisely what he and his friends used to call centralization when they were on this side of the house?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am wondering if under this clause the board is permitted to bring only a part of the difference in price under its control, in the case of a company which owns both the gas and the transmission lines? In this case that would mean the possibility of a much smaller share than in the case of a pipe line company which is merely transporting the gas. I ask this specific question: supposing the company which owns the pipe line also owns the gas. These figures might not be realistic, but supposing the gas going into the pipe line is bought at a price of, say, 30 cents and it is sold out of the pipe line by the company which owns the pipe line and owns the gas to a company that is distributing the gas, to a retail company, at a price of 60 cents. I want to know whether, according to this clause, the difference between 30 and 60, or part of the difference between 30 and 60 can be exempted from this provision. If this is the case I think the clause is wide open for an interpretation by the board which would allow the company to proceed almost free of all regulations. I can understand that if the 30 refers to the price of the gas going into the line and the 60 refers to the price of the gas going to the consumer, this clause would exempt a proportion of the cost which ordinarily might be considered a retailing cost. But my question is this: if the 60 is the price to a distributor is it then possible for the board to say whether or not it should regulate the full difference between the 30 and 60?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is a question which has received a good deal of study. It has arisen in the minds of many people and a great deal of midnight oil was burned over clause 61, I can assure the hon. member. The difference between the 30 he mentioned and 60-the entire amount-the board could take as a differential or it could take any proportion of that which it saw fit in view of all the circumstances and in view of what it considered to be just and reasonable.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister's explanation to me is not satisfactory. It may be an accurate explanation but I take it that the board has the right to decide what proportion it feels it should control in this specific case in view of all the circumstances. I would submit that is a very loosely worded clause. It means in fact that the board could decide to regulate

only a small proportion of the difference in cost and the whole bill, whatever it may be worth,-and as we go from clause to clause I see less and less value in it-would fall to the ground. I do not know why the board is not given the power to regulate the entire difference between the price of gas going into the line and the price of gas coming out of the line.
If the gas pipe-line company is itself in the retail field I think the board would have to set an arbitrary figure as to what should be the price coming out of the line. Under this clause I do not see why the board should be given the power in the instance of a company that owns the gas to exempt most of its operating margin from control.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I am not getting this through my head but I do not want it to pass until I understand it. Is my interpretation of this correct? Does this deal wholly and solely with the transmission of gas on an interprovincial basis purchased in one province and sold in another? Do the words "the board may fix of the differential" mean that the board may decide the differential between the purchase price of the gas at one end and the selling price at the other? Is that basically what it means or is the minister now as confused as I was when I started?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in answer to the hon. member's first question I would say that this does refer to a pipe line crossing a provincial boundary. It reads that the board may fix of the differential between the amount paid by the company for the gas and the amount for which the gas is sold by the company. This means whatever proportion it chooses; the whole thing, if it likes. Using the figure the hon. member for Assiniboia put forward, if it is 30 cents at the intake end and 60 cents at the point where it leaves the pipe and goes to the consumer the difference is 30 cents and the board may say the 30 cents is the toll. On the contrary it could say that of that 30 cents it considers that 25 cents or 20 cents should be the toll charged. The board determines the proportion of the 30 cents that shall be declared to be the toll, but it could be the whole 30 cents.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this clause goes part way to meet the difficulty I raised the other day when we were dealing with another clause of the bill, I believe the clause having to do with the definition of the word "company". In any event, it puts the type of very large pipe line to which I made reference on that occasion under this act in so far as certain rights and privileges of the company are concerned. Some of the rights and privileges given to such a private company incorporated by special act are quite extensive. I would point out-and I want the minister to correct me if I am wrong-that the amendment gives such a private company the very extensive right of expropriation of lands, but at the same time does not protect in any way the public who may be investors in such a pipe line company. We are not giving any protection by way of public hearings by the new board before the company constructs its line. There is no requirement that they apply for a licence, and the fact may well be that such a company will be thought by many of the investing public to be another pipe line company under the jurisdiction and control of the national energy board.
I would point out that the particular company to which I made reference on Friday- and I may say I know very little about it- uses in its name the words "pipe line company", a name very similar to the type of name commonly used by oil and gas transmission lines. We are doing something here that causes me some concern. It is a real point. I must say that I for one dislike intensely the common habit of this parliament and of legislatures in the provincial field of extending the right of expropriation pretty freely, and here we are doing that very thing and at the same time not giving the public the corresponding type of protection that parliament in its wisdom has seen fit to apply to all other pipe lines dealing with the transmission of products arising out of the oil development in the west. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

If the clause is going to stand I would just like to say the few words I intended to say on this clause before it stands. As a matter of fact, I was rising to make the

same comment as the hon. member for Essex East made with respect to what right has this parliament to authorize a company to take land in the name of the queen in the right of a province? I also want to deal with the question of crossing private land. I am thinking particularly of farm land, because we had rather an unfortunate experience in our district in the laying of a pipe line there. I notice that this clause, particularly in paragraphs (b) and (c), makes provision for a company to purchase, take and hold of and from any person any land or other property necessary for the construction, maintenance and operation of its pipe line and alienate, sell or dispose of any of its land or property that for any reason has become unnecessary for the purpose of the line.
Paragraph (c) reads:
Construct, lay, carry or place Its pipe line across, upon or under the land ot any person on the located line of the pipe line.
When I go to clause 68 I notice there appears to be more protection given to mining companies. Clause 68 reads:
No company shall, without the authority of the board, locate the line of its proposed pipe line, or construct the pipe line or portion thereof, so as to obstruct or interfere with or injuriously affect the working of or the access or adit to a mine then open, or for the opening of which preparations are, at the time of such location, being lawfully and openly made.
My point is that there appears to be much greater protection provided under the legislation for a mining company, or mining operations, than there is for a farmer. In our section during the construction of a pipe line the engineers for a certain company laid out the route, and this route was over a distance of some 15 miles just beside a highway, some 100 feet back from the highway, but in front of a considerable number of farm residences, and in some instances going within 10 feet of the farmers' verandahs and through their barnyards along this considerable distance. When the local people, the owners, protested, the engineer in charge said, "No, we have got the right and that is where the line is going." When the people of Kootenay West are in trouble it is only natural that they come to the member for Kootenay West under such circumstances and at that time they did so although this was a provincial matter. I went and saw the farmers and told them not to sign anything. The engineer in question threw the easement document on the ground and said, "If you will not sign it we will go to court and get the right very quickly." I said to the farmers, "Do not sign anything".
I called a meeting of all these people. They all happened to be members of the Doukhobor sect although not Sons of Freedom. At the meeting they discussed their problem and they
National Energy Board had a legitimate complaint. Fortunately we were able to have the matter considered by a prominent lawyer in Vancouver. He went to see the attorney general who saw the injustice and called in the heads of the company and as a result of what in effect was almost an order they had to change the route of the line to the back of the farms which all bordered on mountain ground. The area is between Brilliant and South Slocan and the Minister of Public Works understands exactly what I am talking about.
There was no provision there for reference to a board or anything of that sort. Apparently they had the right to do this. It was only after meetings, united opposition and the realization on the part of the government that this was a very unwise thing to do in that county, to say the least, that the company concerned was forced to change the location of the line at an increased cost of $30,000 to $40,000. I think we should do everything possible to make certain that the rights of farmers and small property holders are protected. In another case this company went right through a man's farm, and with an oil pipe line it is not simply a question of burying the pipe. A certain area of ground on each side of the pipe cannot be cultivated or used and has to be kept free of weeds so that if gas escapes it will not be inflammable. There are several disabilities to property owners who, in my opinion, are not sufficiently covered just by the payment of so much per acre for the land used.
Because of my experience in this respect and the experience of some of my constituents I should like the minister to explain to the committee what protection there is in this clause for the farmer or small property holder in order to prevent a recurrence of such circumstances and also why more protection apparently is provided to mining companies than to farmers and small property holders when it comes to the question of entering their property for the laying of a pipe line.

I wonder if I could address myself briefly to clause 79? Contrary to some prognostications that there is nothing new in this bill, this is an innovation and one upon which the government is to be commended in my humble estimate. Briefly, this clause provides that subcontractors, suppliers and workmen who, unfortunately, have not been paid, may attach a lien under the various provincial statutes to contractors' claims. We had an unfortunate experience a few years ago during the construction of an interprovincial pipe line when a substantial subcontractor was unable to collect because he was not able to file his lien. I think it would be highly unfair that while pipe lines within provinces are subject to the right of every citizen to recover in respect of unpaid claims, promoters of a pipe line which crosses a boundary should escape such responsibilities.
It must, of course, be recognized that the right to file a lien is subject to the statutes and provisions which exist within each province. I do not think there are good grounds for the fear expressed by some people that this provision may harass the pipe line companies. I do not think this will necessarily follow, and I submit that this is an excellent provision.

that nothing in this act restricts or prohibits any of the following transactions-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say on clause 83 which, notwithstanding the amendment which has been introduced by the minister, is very important as far as this bill is concerned. Clause 83 imposes on the board the duty of having regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant though no such duty is imposed under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. We have no objection to this change but clause 83 also requires the board to ensure that the quantity of gas or power to be exported does not exceed the surplus remaining after allowance has been made for the foreseeable requirements for use in Canada.
When the Prime Minister spoke on second reading of this bill he insisted that the bill was introduced to protect the public interest. We feel there is no clause in this bill which protects the public interest from the tolls to be charged in comparison with those that could be charged when such commodities are exported. I therefore move:
That paragraph (b) of section 83 of Bill C-49 be replaced by the following:
83(b) the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is not lower than the price at which gas or power, respectively, is supplied by him or his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada.
My main reason for introducing this amendment is that in certain cases power is being exported and sold to consumers in the United States. There is no provision in the bill to give assurance that the rates charged to United States consumers will be comparable to those charged Canadian consumers. We think the best illustration can be found in New Brunswick where the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission exports power to the state of Maine where a certain company exports in turn this same power to Canadian consumers along the Saint John river valley. We feel there should be protection under which Canadian consumers would not be charged rates exceeding those charged United States consumers and

under which a Canadian company exporting power to the United States would not charge rates lower than those it would charge Canadian consumers for the same power.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I pass one observation on the amendment. Surely the hon. member who proposes this amendment must realize that market conditions in the two countries may be entirely different. The United States distributor may be competing with other types of power or fuel which are not applicable in Canada. How could the Canadian government absolutely determine what the ultimate rate would be to the consumer in the United States? Once a contract has been established there may be a change in the situation. Whereas in Canada the rates may be allowed to go up after various hearings, in the United States the rates might be driven down by reason of competition or otherwise; yet the hon. member would forbid export under those circumstances. I feel that the hon. gentleman is getting into some horrible difficulties.

speechtext:
It will also give the Conservatives an opportunity to fulfil an election promise made in British Columbia. I was reading in the paper a few moments ago that the Minister of Justice was speaking in British Columbia and boasting about how many promises the Conservatives had implemented. In British Columbia the Conservatives promised that there would be placed on the statute books of Canada a piece of legislation that would never again allow a situation like that which presently obtains in that province. Gas in Alberta and northern British Columbia is shipped all across the province of British Columbia on one line which remains unbroken until it reaches a point approximately fifty miles from Vancouver where it divides two ways. It goes to New Westminster, Burnaby and Vancouver through one branch and across the border through the other. The price to the wholesaler at the border on gas going south of the border is less per thousand cubic feet than the price to the wholesaler who supplies it to Canadian citizens in Vancouver, New Westminster, Burnaby and the Fraser valley.
This is an extraordinary and damnable situation which the Conservatives during the election said they were going to correct. Through this amendment we want to make sure a correction takes place. We are certainly in support of this amendment and we feel that the Conservatives are, too, unless they have changed their minds in the last two years.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The amendment that has been proposed is almost identical in wording with regulation 9 under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. This is the regulation which the Borden commission recommended should be rescinded. Recommendation No. 4 of the Borden report reads as follows:
That regulation 9 of "Regulations respecting the exportation of power and fluids and the importation of gas" made and established by order in council P.C. 1955-907, in so far as it applies to natural gas, be rescinded.
My hon. friends, now faced with that, are attempting to have it re-established in the legislation. That regulation is precisely the one which gave rise to the difficulties out at the west coast because of the phrasing, "in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale", and it is very difficult to get two situations exactly similar. For that reason, along with other things that we have done in the legislation, we have left it to the board to determine what is just and reasonable in the circumstances; is it just and reasonable with regard to the price to be

National Energy Board
charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him, and it is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
The board we think will have to take into account the very factors my hon. friends are pointing out as to whether the public interest is protected, and to make sure that Canadians are not placed at a disadvantage with regard to their competitors in the United States. Our experience in Canada dates back to the days long before gas was used in this country, when hydroelectric power was being developed, and when hydroelectric power was being developed in this country some of it was done by United States capital. The power was exported across the line and used to build up United States industry there. Many years ago our people discovered that the advantage lay with the United States using the power that was developed in Canada. With that experience behind us we do not want to have the same thing happen with regard to this other great source of energy, namely natural gas.
Surely this is something that the energy board will take into account when it is considering the applications for export. At the same time I am sure they will have to take into consideration the cost to Canadian consumers if there is no export of gas. A line built at tremendous expense might operate at only a fraction of its total efficiency unless some gas were exported. If it operates lower than its full efficiency, obviously the price to the Canadian consumer will rise. The board will have to weigh and balance these factors one against the other and see what is to the advantage of Canada. With the difficulties that have already arisen and are apparent to Canadians under regulation No. 9 which I have just read we thought the wise thing to do was to give the board freedom of action to weigh all those factors and determine what was just and reasonable in relation to the public interest, and that is why the clause is worded as it is.
