speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to say just a few words about the sale of electrical power across the border. I think there is some misunderstanding in the mind of the hon. member for Gloucester on this score because I have been in conversation with the New Brunswick electric power commission and with other power commissions in various parts of the country. It is very clear to me that in the sale of hydroelectric power you have to keep in mind three or four types of power. If you are talking about firm power which will sell under a base load obviously it would be very simple to have the type of amendment you have in mind. Basic power can be sold at lower rates in the country of the source of origin sometimes.
You come now to the question of secondary power either as peak or dump power. If you can get a contract for your secondary power sometimes it can be sold at a lower price in your home country; but if you are up against a situation whereby your power surplus has a dumping factor in it then you do have to sell any place. This dumping

power comes up without any knowledge simply because of the flow or lack of demand. Then, it is customary in power systems to get rid of this power at any price whatever and that, of course, is the case in the New Brunswick electric power commission, the example which the hon. member gave. Last year because of the high flows in the Saint John river they had a power surplus beyond all their expected demands and beyond all they could use in their own country. Therefore, rather than let the power go to waste they sold it to the systems to the south for what I consider was an attractive price of five mills.
Therefore, getting back to the amendment, if you put in an amendment-and I can interrupt myself here by saying that no person more than I wanted, in all the cases listed, something that would prevent the things I complained of in the last few years-when you take a look at the direct benefit, if you put the amendment in that you have to sell at a lower price for similar quantities, then in the case of electric power you can do great harm to the efficiency of the Canadian-operated system. If we are to measure ourselves as to how good Canadians we are I think the test should be one that gives the best for Canadian interests all along the line. In the case of hydro power, when you are referring to dump power particularly, it would be absolutely wrong and hurt Canadian interests if you put such a statutory proviso in the bill which would limit the board to make adjustments that would be advantageous to Canada.
The same thing could apply to natural gas. No person in this house has over the years stood up and complained more about what has happened with the Westcoast Transmission and could have happened at Emerson and may even happen at the Niagara connection of those United States competitors who are processing using Canadian power cheaper than we in Canada can get it. If you limit this board to regulation 9 in the old act you might legally allow the very thing to happen that happened before, and I think we should all be determined not to let that happen again in the future.

speechtext:
I am sure we have listened to a very extraordinary argument by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in support of the clause as it is proposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As has just been pointed out, the conditions and circumstances of the foreign sale of gas, which have been mentioned by the hon. gentleman, can be safeguarded in the public interest by bearing in mind the concluding words in the proposed amendment which bear repetition, namely "is supplied by him or his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada."
The hon. gentleman has made the same argument that was made by his colleague who argues for what he calls the principle of flexibility or perhaps we should more accurately say the principle of doubt. If the Canadian interest is such that the situation is as revealed by the two ministers speaking for the government, then surely the necessary safeguards are provided in the concluding part of this amendment. We have had placed on Hansard tonight the words of the Minister of Public Works, words uttered by him as a responsible member of the party in power. Those words must be taken as reflecting the principles that the

National Energy Board government had in mind with regard to this measure, and if there could be any doubt about the authority of this position the Leader of the Opposition has removed that by referring to the observations made by the Prime Minister in his speech on the bill on May 26 last when he said on this very point, as the Leader of the Opposition reminded us, as found at page 4025 of Hansard:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interest. With the implementation of this legislation, no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer-
These are the important words.
-is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their energy than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy.
With the safeguard in the amendment, "in similar quantities and under similar conditions", how is it possible for the government tonight to persist in this particular clause in the face of this statement by the Prime Minister? The Prime Minister is the head of the government and if hon. gentlemen pursue the present clause in its present form we are confronted with a division of view in the ministry itself. The Prime Minister had no doubts about this matter. I refer to other words of his which will be found on page 4021 of Hansard in which he said:
Finally there is the question of whether the public interest will be protected. One of the matters that was the cause of infinite unfairness to Canadians under some of the licences granted when the former government was in power was that Canadians paid through the nose for consumption in Canada while the price in the United States was lower.
These are not the words of a private member among those who sit on Mr. Speaker's right. These are not merely the words of a minister of the crown. These are the words of the Prime Minister spoken in this very debate on this very bill. When the Prime Minister spoke his words went all through the country. They were widely reported as reflecting the opinion of the government and these words of the Prime Minister were also widely applauded. The Prime Minister cannot expect parliament or the Canadian people to accept his words as representing government policy if the amendment now before the committee is not accepted or if there is no other appropriate modification of the words in the existing clause. The Prime Minister went on to say on page 4021:
These are a few of the material matters with which this legislation is concerned. Somebody said that the powers should be spelled out. In reply I affirm that they are spelled out-
We are asking that they be spelled out. We are asking that under similar conditions

where there are similar quantities involved Canadians will not be charged more than citizens or industrial corporations of the United States. That is the principle, that they shall be treated alike. That is what the Prime Minister said. Our amendment carries forward the principle stated in the Prime Minister's observations. The bill as now drawn without this amendment is absolutely contrary to what the Prime Minister said. I can only say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has carefully piloted this legislation and, if I may say so, has done so with an understanding of the position of those who have sought to improve it, that he is placed in the invidious position of putting forward a clause in a bill which is diametrically opposed to the statements to which I have referred and which were made by the Prime Minister in his speech on this bill.

This is the important point.
-was that Canadians paid through the nose for consumption in Canada while the price in the United States was lower.
These words are on all fours with this amendment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce tonight, in putting forward this particular clause in its present form, presents to the house the most unusual sight of cabinet division that we have seen since this government came into office. The Prime Minister is advocating a policy that is fully consistent with this amendment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is advocating another policy. He might not have recalled the words of the Prime Minister, and it is because of that that I hope he has taken advantage of the reading of those words of the Prime Minister to reflect on the position in which I think he is unfairly placed. Under our system of government, the cabinet must speak with one voice. The Prime Minister, on a matter of policy, cannot have one view and one or more of his ministers another.

If the Minister of Trade and Commerce persists in presenting this clause, without the amendment or the kind of amendment proposed, then hon. members and the country-can come to no other conclusion but that the cabinet is divided on this matter, and the consequences of such a division of ministerial view are well known to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

-that he has seen. As a matter of fact, the entire house is in agreement on the principle of this matter, the principle being that Canadians shall not be placed at a disadvantage when their natural resource, gas, is exported. We are in agreement upon that, but my hon. friends want to continue as the law of the land regulation No. 9 which I read some time ago. They want to continue this regulation which has caused all the trouble.
This regulation was examined by the Borden commission and they rejected it. They said to rescind it. Let me quote to you what the royal commission on energy had to say on page 13 of their first report. After reprinting the regulation, the commission wrote as follows:
While the commission believes it understands the result which regulation 9 was designed to accomplish, nevertheless we have found it most difficult and, indeed, almost impossible to interpret. In the first place, the quantities and conditions of natural gas sales vary greatly as between contracts, so that price comparisons are difficult to make. The usual method of determining appropriate prices is based on a computation of cost of service and there are various methods of allocating certain of these costs to different types and quantities of sale. Furthermore, the regulation does not take into account other factors, such as competitive prices and value of service, factors which many authorities believe should be taken into account in the setting of prices. In the opinion of the commission, regulation 9 should be rescinded.
The commission believes that, if a national energy board enquires into the terms and conditions of each proposed export contract, satisfies itself that the terms are fair and reasonable and in the public interest, and discharges the other responsibilities which the commission is recommending should be placed upon it, the objectives which the commission assumes were envisaged by regulation 9 will be achieved.
Regulation 9, as the hon. member for Kootenay West pointed out, is the regulation under which the situation developed about which he complained. The Prime Minister drew attention to this regulation on page 4021 of Hansard for May 26, 1959. He said this:
Members of the former administration said, "We cannot protect you because the regulations say that
National Energy Board
regard must be had to similar conditions and similar quantities before determination in this regard can be made."
It is because regulation 9 did not give the protection that everybody wants, and the whole House of Commons is in agreement on this, that the Borden commission rejected regulation 9 and suggested another way of dealing with it. Our drafting of the bill is made to achieve exactly that desired end. We put it up to the energy board to size up all the factors concerning each contract for export and determine, as it says here, that the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest. The public interest means the Canadian public interest, and surely the public interest means the development of Canadian industry. This does not mean to make it possible for a competitor across the line to gain an advantage from the use of our natural resource, gas.
How is it to be done? Regulation 9 has been tried and has been found wanting, so the suggestion is that the board be given this power to determine the method by which the public interest can be protected. It was not protected under regulation 9. My hon. friends, who are striving to bring regulation 9 back into the statutes, are surely on the wrong track. This has been proven to be wrong. The regulation was examined by the Borden commission and rejected and a new method suggested which is calculated to do exactly the things that regulation 9 did not do, one of which is to protect the public interest. I have read and re-read regulation 9, which is really the amendment before us. There is a change in only one or two words. Regulation 9 falls on that phrase, "in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale", because you cannot get those things exactly equal. A person who is buying in great bulk, as was done out on the west coast, is buying under different conditions from the person who is operating a very small business on the Canadian side. This was the argument under regulation 9, that prices for export, therefore, should be lower than the prices in our own country, and it is to that the people are objecting.
Then how do we get the safeguard? Our suggestion is embodied in this clause with which we have been dealing, clause 83, paragraph (b). This will give us the safeguard that everyone wants. Certainly we cannot get it if we just simply carry along with regulation 9. My hon. friends, therefore, who have been trying to make out a case of

National Energy Board cabinet disunity and a case for lack of concern with regard to the Canadian people, have been arguing from a false premise. Our concern is exactly the same as that of our hon. friends opposite. Our concern was expressed by the Prime Minister in the words that have been quoted and re-quoted. Our concern has been shown by the wording which we have put into this bill.

I just wanted to say a few words on this amendment. I was rather surprised at the example cited by the hon. member for Gloucester in support of his amendment. He cited the export of electricity or power from the province of New Brunswick. He knows as well as I do that there is very little power exported from New Brunswick, an infinitesimal amount. As a matter of fact, up until the time the present government in New Brunswick came into power New Brunswick was starved for power. We feel very proud today that we not only have sufficient power for our own use but last year, as was pointed out by the minister for northern affairs, had power to export.
If we had charged the same price for the power that was exported as we charged for the power that was used we would not have been able to sell it. It would have been an entire loss. I suppose we used about 95 per cent at least of the power that was produced. The other small quantity was exported. The New Brunswick power commission found that they could make a good sale in the United States. They were well satisfied. I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that the people of New Brunswick felt that the public interest was well served by the amount that they received. I think that had this act with this proposed amendment been in force at that time the province of New Brunswick would have lost the sale of this amount of power and would have had this surplus on its hands. Frankly, as I said a few moments ago, I feel that a great disservice would have been done to the province of New Brunswick which is today in the proud position of obtaining all the power that it needs and, in addition, has some to export.

Is he going to discriminate against the buyers in the province of New Brunswick simply in order to satisfy the sale of a very small quantity of power abroad?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think this matter can rest at this point because the principle involved is too important. It will be recalled that when the Prime Minister spoke on May 26 he was followed by the hon. member for Ottawa West who put on the record a statement my Mr. John Davis who wrote in the "Behind the Headlines" series a pamphlet entitled "Canadian Energy Policy". At page 6, in the second last complete

paragraph, in the last sentence of that study, the following appears: He goes on to point out:
The quantities of energy used in both countries-
That is Canada and the United States.
-are about the same per unit of gross national product. Hence, the basic difference is one of price. Even in 1958, consumers in Canada were paying between 30 and 50 per cent more for their energy than were their opposite numbers in the U.S.A.
At that time we were discussing the second reading of the bill. We had not reached an examination clause by clause of the measure as we are now doing tonight. What the Leader of the Opposition and those of us who have spoken on this point have been endeavouring to do is to point out that the head of the government has taken one position and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is taking another. In the absence of a statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce I think we can only conclude that the point of view stated by the Prime Minister is for some reason or another not now being accepted by the government.
The Leader of the Opposition has put on the record observations made by the Prime Minister in his speech during this debate and a few moments ago I put on the record another statement of his. I now wish to put on the record a third statement which was made by the Prime Minister and which is seemingly even stronger and more pertinent than were the other two and only accentuates the difference that prevails between my hon. friend who has the responsibility of piloting this measure and the Prime Minister.
As reported at pages 4025 and 4026 of Hansard the Prime Minister stated as follows:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interests. With the implementation of this legislation, no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their industries than those paid by foreign energy using Canadian energy. That matter is extremely important.
Then the Prime Minister went on to say this, and I underline these words:
In the trade world in which we are living, with the conflicts that are accelerating from month to month in the communist trade offensive, above everything else it is necessary for us in Canada, if our international trade is to be maintained, to see to it that we shall not be placed in a position where our costs in connection with energy derived from Canada are greater to Canadians than they are to any other nation, however friendly that nation may be.
Can there be any doubt about those words? The head of the government says that we must take steps in the bill, second reading
National Energy Board of which was then before the house, so as to see to it that we shall not be placed in a position where our costs in connection with energy derived from Canada are greater to Canadians than they are to any other nation, however friendly that nation may be. Those are the words of the Prime Minister. Either those words mean something or they do not. Either they meant something when they were uttered or they were intended to give an impression which I am sure the Prime Minister did not intend. But the only conclusion is that his indications of intention are not being carried out in this bill. All that is being provided for in section 83 is that the board shall have regard to all considerations et cetera and that the board shall satisfy itself that the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
That is not what the Prime Minister said. The clause before us is not a direction. It is simply an indication that in considering an application for gas or power export the board will determine whether or not the price to be charged is just and reasonable. It says nothing about the price being charged to foreign corporations or industries being the same as the price being charged to Canadians.
Unless the minister is able to reconcile the difference between the words of the Prime Minister and the terms of this bill, the minister guiding this legislation tonight is, I repeat, in the unfortunate position of proposing something which represents a serious division between himself and the Prime Minister. The minister smiles, and I can understand why he should smile-I can understand his desire to smile-but that does not alter the fact that there is this difference between him, in his bill, and the words of the Prime Minister and this, under our constitutional practice, requires from the minister an explanation of the reasons for that variation in opinion which he has not yet given to the committee.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is very entertaining indeed, but he is not logical and I regret that, because he used to be logical. There is no difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and myself. If there were I should be happy to find it out from the Prime Minister and not from hon. gentlemen opposite.
The words of the Prime Minister have often been quoted. He pointed out in his statement on May 26 that regulation 9 had failed to

National Energy Board give Canadians the protection they required. He stated in the same speech:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.

speechtext: No, no.

speechtext:
Almost word for word. The hon. gentleman says "no" but let me read out part of clause 83:
The price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
That is what the Prime Minister had in mind, that the public interest would be protected by giving this type of authority to the energy board who would not be cribbed, cabined and confined by regulation No. 9 which is a restrictive regulation. Here the board can take account of all the factors which should be considered, and there is no no doubt in my mind, after the Borden report and after the lengthy discussion here in the House of Commons, but that the energy board to be set up will take fully into account the Canadian national interest and take fully into account the expressions of opinion here from both sides of the committee, leading toward the same objective.
I commend hon. members opposite for their helpfulness in discussion throughout this debate. They have been of assistance to us in clarifying the measure. I think, however, that in this particular instance they have been somewhat less than helpful, although they have very clearly stated that in their opinion the national interest requires the same thing as we consider that the national interest requires. Thus we are at one as far as that goes. We differ as to the wording by which that objective is to be achieved. I see no difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and myself with regard to the substance of clause 83.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister one question, if I may. What objection could the government have to accepting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gloucester unless he and his colleagues intend that energy should be sold at a lower price to the United States? What conceivable objection could there be to this amendment unless it is intended to sell at a cheaper price to the United States?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should read this clause into the record in order to make my argument clear:
84. (1) Subject to subsection (2) and the regulations, the board may by order revoke or suspend a licence issued under this part if, in the opinion of the board, the person to whom it was issued has violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof.
(2) No order shall be made under this section unless notice has been given to the holder of the licence who is alleged to have violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof and an opportunity has been afforded to him of being heard.
My point is this. Presumably on these licences there may be several terms and conditions, some very important and some of lesser importance. It is possible that an exporter or a person licensed under this part may inadvertently fail to carry out one of the terms or conditions attached to the licence.

This present cause provides that he would be given notice and an opportunity of being heard. The legislation on which this is modelled is section 3 of the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act.
That act provided that in addition to their being a breach there must be notice to the licensee and the licensee must have an opportunity of rectifying the matter when drawn to his attention, and if he rectifies it there was no power of revocation. I point out to the minister the same argument I made on clause 47 which is similar when I outlined the danger of what he is doing by taking away that right of a licensee to rectify his breach in those circumstances.
I could perhaps move an amendment similar to that I moved previously but I do not think it is necessary. I made the point on the similar clause and I believe it is well understood by the committee. What the minister is doing here is putting an uncertainty on the value of these licences and that value is going to impair the right of the holder of the licence to finance his enterprise.
The minister pointed out at some length the need for investment in this whole industry and in the development of the sources of energy with which we are concerned and yet by this clause he is doing something that will interfere with obtaining investment and indeed tend to prevent the realization of what he indicated on second reading was so necessary. I therefore want to again draw the attention and point out this defect in the clause.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was not certain that the hon. member wanted me to comment at length on this. I appreciate that his argument is the same as he made so effectively on clause 47. We have written in here the opportunity for the holder of the licence to be heard under the circumstances. If his licence is to be revoked or suspended notice must be given and an opportunity for him to be heard must also be given. We think that provides adequate protection. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, subclause 2
of clause 85 reads as follows:
66968-9-269
National Energy Board
The governor in council may by regulation exempt any person or class of persons or any product or class of products or any transactions, persons or areas from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this part or the regulations.
It seems to me that this is another of those paragraphs that gives sweeping powers to the governor in council under which in fact, if the governor in council wished, it could take away all of the powers the board has under this clause. I think it is perfectly ridiculous for parliament to go to great lengths to spell out the specific powers of the energy board which the government says is going to be staffed by competent men and then include provisions of this kind.
Part VI in my opinion contains sufficient qualifications and escape hatches for the board to make decisions in the interest of Canada. I do not know why the governor in council should wish to retain this allembracing power. I therefore move:
That subclause 2 of clause 85 be deleted.
If the governor in council wishes to strengthen the powers of the board the members of the cabinet should have no hesitation in accepting this amendment. They have been in a receptive mood as far as some suggestions are concerned. If the board is going to be competent surely the cabinet does not need to retain this complete power of veto over every action of the board.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Once again in relation to
this clause there appears to be in the mind of the hon. member a tendency to go beyond what was intended. If it seems suitable to parliament to accept the subsequent clause No. 87 and if in time oil becomes controlled as to export and import, unless exemptions are permitted there would be an endless amount of red tape in the issuing of permits and licences for a product which would be moving not only by pipe line-in which form it is easy to control-but moving in small quantities, in tins and in forms like that.
Without an exemption provided for in the regulations every single bit of oil including the small cans of sewing machine oil would have to come in by permit. It was to guard against red tape and a great increase in the number of people who would be required to administer a program like that that this exemption clause was written in.
If my hon. friend thinks that it destroys the power of the board, or that the governor in council might be somewhat arbitrary in its use, there is always the responsibility surely to the House of Commons and to parliament. The government has to answer for everything that it does, so there is a check, and an effective check, on the misuse-which my hon. friend is thinking of-of subclause (2) of clause 85.

National Energy Board

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we on this side of the house are definitely in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member. speechtext: The hon. member did not catch my last phrase, "from actual experience".

Hidden reports; cabinet secrecy.
We have a bill before us, Mr. Chairman, setting up an energy board, and every important decision is subject to the approval of the cabinet. Surely the cabinet, in carrying out the public business of the country under its jurisdiction, has a tremendous burden now without having this all-embracing power which the Minister of Trade and Commerce says will be used only on trivial matters. I think the whole purpose in setting up this energy board should have been to give to the energy board the right to make important decisions which are not subject to cabinet veto every day of the week. There are certain things I would not object to, such as an appeal on general rates to the cabinet as there is on freight rates now from the board of transport commissioners; but to have

every single decision of the energy board subject to cabinet approval I think would be a very great mistake. The cabinet complains of its burdens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we on this side would have moved the same amendment that has been put forward by the C.C.F. if they had not done it because this is an extraordinary provision to have in legislation of this kind, particularly as it comes from the Minister of Trade and Commerce who used to talk so vigorously and violently on the rights of parliament and the necessity of reducing the power of the executive.
The minister has said, of course, that their intentions in the exercise of this particular power will be good but, as the minister must surely recognize, good intentions do not ensure good legislation. He has also said-and this is a most extraordinary argument-that the reason for this provision is so that the cabinet can protect the public interest against unnecessary red tape and all that kind of thing. In other words, we are setting up a board of five responsible members. We are giving that board great powers, and yet the governor in council cannot entrust this particular board with enough power to deal with those minor matters. They must themselves put a provision in the legislation allowing the cabinet to take from the board not only its powers in minor matters but all powers because this particular clause empowers the governor in council to exempt any person or class of persons or any product or class of products or any transactions persons or areas

from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this part or the regulations. If that is not an arrogation unto itself by the executive of all powers over legislation, then I do not know what arrogation of power means. The only excuse the minister has given us, or the only one he has given us so far, is that there may be some quantities of this and that come in, some kind of oil, some kind of gas.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Cod liver oil.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Cod liver oil or castor oil. It would not do to have this board wasting its time on matters of this kind; we have to give this kind of thing to the cabinet. Surely in the circumstances the minister himself will realize that this provision is not only unnecessary but ridiculous, and if it is not ridiculous it is dangerous.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This matter is too important to allow it to pass without further observation, particularly in the absence of a strong statement from the minister.
The clause before us gives the governor in council power to make regulations for carrying into effect the purposes and provisions of this part and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing to make regulations respecting (a), (b), (c), (d), and so on. Usually, where the board or a minister or the governor in council is empowered to make regulations there is a provision for the tabling of those regulations. There is nothing in this legislation or the regulations requiring the governor in council or the minister to table the regulations within 15 days of the opening of parliament. I well remember the criticism which was levelled by hon. members over alleged assumption of power by the executive, by the present Minister of Justice.
We were going to give to a board, I think it was the old age pensions board, the power to make regulations, and those regulations the country and parliament would never know about. It was argued they would be kept within the confines of the knowledge of officials from the provinces or the federal government. There must be a requirement of the ministry, it was argued, that these regulations shall be tabled so that parliament will know what they are.
If there was justification, and there was, for that argument, how much more there is for a measure of this sort affecting as it does civil liberties and civil rights of the greatest kind. I suggest to the minister that on his own initiative he will see the force of this argument and that he will take steps to modify this clause at once so that there will be a requirement to table in parliament within a 66968-9-269J
National Energy Board specified number of days the regulations which the governor in council will be empowered to make.
With regard to subclause 2, certainly there ought to be a requirement for the tabling of such a regulation. That subclause reads:
The governor in council may by regulation exempt any person or class of persons or any product or class of products or any transactions, persons or areas from the operation of all or any of the provisions of this part or the regulations.
Yet there is no requirement to table a regulation so fundamental in its implications. I hope that the minister will take the initiative, as I said, to make provision in the bill for tabling the regulations envisaged in subclause 1 and in subclause 2. What can be the purpose of this particular clause? Here we have decided to pick a board, not a board of three as was suggested from this side in the interests of economy but a board of five, of five of the best and most competent individuals who can be obtained.

speechtext: Already selected.

speechtext:
Already selected, one hon. member suggests-a board that is going to have the powers covered by various clauses we have already dealt with, and all of a sudden in one of the concluding clauses of the bill the governor in council takes the power to vitiate in whole or in part anything that the board may have done.
Let us just see how far-reaching this clause is. It is one thing to have government by the executive and parliament but under our system it is another thing to have government only by the executive. How often have we heard the Minister of Justice, who laughs now, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and others, speak about preserving the rights of parliament? I do not recall the Minister of National Defence in this particular but I am sure the Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland was among those who spoke feverishly about preserving the rights of parliament against an executive that wanted to assume exclusive power. Hon. gentlemen have the opportunity tonight to repeat their speeches. Let them look at this particular clause and observe the power given to the executive by a government that was going to preserve the rights of parliament at all times, a government headed by a right hon. gentleman who went up and down the length and breadth of the country complaining about the invasion of the rights of parliament by the preceding government. Yet this present government, with less than two years in office, comes to parliament and puts before us a clause like this, the like of which perhaps no government in the history of Canada has ever tried to put before parliament.

National Energy Board

object. I see the hon. member lor Rosedale laughing. He is a lawyer and one who theoretically at any rate, and I am sure in fact, appreciates the value of the rule of law. I ask the Prime Minister now: Do you have to circumvent the rule of law in order to achieve power under this legislation? Nothing of the kind! Have the powers, but in order to assure-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: My hon. friends laugh. of the individual but at the same time they want this power of veto. They have not told us why. I ask him tonight as Minister of Justice, in charge of the law offices of the crown, as the minister supposed to advise his colleagues on those matters that have to do with preserving the rule of law, what does he think of a clause in a bill that gives to the governor in council the power by a single act, an order in council based on a regulation that need not be tabled in the house-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Certainly, it must be tabled.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it must be tabled. Will he point out where, in this clause, there is anything that requires the governor in council to table a regulation or where there is anything in this clause that requires the governor in council to table particular regulations exempting any class or any person or any class of persons or any product or class of products or any transactions, persons or areas from the operations of all or any of the provisions of this part of the regulations.
Talk about government by executive-I say again there has never been-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Has my hon. friend never heard of the Regulations Act?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: -on the part of any government less appreciation of the importance of its relationship to parliament. What was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Has my hon. friend never heard of the Regulations Act when he says there is no provision that these regulations shall be tabled?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend says, have I heard of the Regulations Act? Of course I have heard of the Regulations Act, but I have also seen acts that insist upon a board having this power also making it mandatory that these regulations be tabled. I have seen other acts under which the governor in council had to take such powers as these, making these bodies responsible to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know the provisions of the Regulations Act?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend says, do I know this or do I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The answer is obvious, you do not.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend not know that one of his first responsibilities as Minister of Justice is to see that the executive arm of government in this country is given powers consistent with the traditional role of the executive in relation to parliament, and powers which will not place the executive in a position where it is capable of overriding the wishes of parliament, the wishes of the people in the country, by order in council? I say to the Minister of Justice, pass this clause and you will have given the best demonstration of the insincerity of the words used by hon. members opposite when they criticized us with regard to legislation which they thought was a violation of the rule of law.
Hon. gentlemen now have the opportunity of proving their worth by changing this clause and making it consistent with the declarations of the Prime Minister and of hon. members who sit opposite, declarations made in this house when they were the great champions of the rights of the people and the rights of parliament itself.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Justice finds this very amusing. Let me put on the record-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I find my hon. friends amusing, not the subject.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Let me put on the record-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is your lieutenant not good enough?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: -what the minister himself had to say on June 13, 1955. What was that witty intervention?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Is your lieutenant not good enough?
National Energy Board

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: He is back to his dreams.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is the kind of intellectual intervention which we are accustomed to expect from my hon. friend. That is what the Minister of Justice had to say on June 13, 1955, page 4732 of Hansard:
Those who give and those who receive arbitrary power are alike criminal and there is no man but is bound to resist it to the best of his power, whenever it shall show its face in the world. It is a crime to bear it when it can be rationally shaken off . . . Law and arbitrary power are in dreadful enmity.
I suggest the Minister of Justice ought to shake off some of this arbitrary power.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when I was listening to the hon. member for Essex East rising to those heights of oratory I saw before me what I had often hoped to see, a member of the House of Commons exhibiting, the meaning of that classic phrase that I think was used by Winston Churchill with respect to a member of the House of Commons being carried away by the exuberance of his own verbosity.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That was Disraeli.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but I believe it was repeated by Winston Churchill. Tonight the hon. member was carried away off the beaten path, away from the root of the matter. He became frightfully excited over what he tried to make out was a vital matter. The Minister of Justice and I were quite pleased at his reference to the debates of 1955. The Minister of Justice said to me, apparently we taught them a lesson which they have not forgotten. Now, they are making us immortal by quoting those words that we spoke in 1955 concerning the rights of parliament,
I should like to mention one or two of the matters referred to by the hon. member for Essex East, the first one of which was with regard to the tabling of the regulations. This is required by the Regulations Act, section 7 of which reads as follows:
Every regulation shall be laid before parliament within 15 days after it is published in the Canada Gazette or, if parliament is not then in session, within 15 days after the commencement of the next ensuing session.
The regulations, therefore, will be made public. They will be disclosed to parliament. They can be called into question by my hon. friends, if they so desire.
My hon. friends attempted to make us believe that this proposed subclause of clause 85 would take away rights which we have already declared to exist for citizens under clause 18. It has nothing to do with that at all and does not remove any rights whatever. Let us descend from the summit and get down to the facts that are involved. Here we are

National Energy Board dealing with part VI, dealing with exports and imports; that is all. We are not dealing with certificates of public convenience and necessity or any of those major matters that the board has to determine. We are dealing here with exports and imports of gas and we suggest that here, by regulation, certain exemptions may be allowed, not for the purpose of burdening the cabinet, as the hon. member for Assiniboia was trying to make out. These regulations will express where the exemptions shall lie and will remove, as I said before, or prevent a great deal of red tape being accumulated in the issuance of permits for small quantities that are exported or imported. Surely, this is a sensible arrangement.
If we accepted the suggestion of my hon. friends in Her Majesty's loyal opposition they would give all the power to the board. We have been debating this back and forth now for seven or eight days, as to who is to have the power. Some of my hon. friends opposite want to give full power to the board. We say it is more sensible to give the board certain powers subject to approval by the governor in council because, the government being responsible to parliament, that is where the responsibility should lie.
However, let us not magnify the importance of subclause (2) of clause 85 which deals with regulations to provide exemptions and simply makes it easier to operate this act under conditions, if and when clause 87 is applied and controls are exercised over oil. This power would not be required to anything like the same extent with regard to gas.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister concludes his argument by appealing to us to leave the section intact on the grounds it would make it easier to operate this act. I do not believe the test of legislation is whether or not it is easy for a government to operate an act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Not for the government, easier for industry.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I hope the minister, when he reads his words, will not put on them the meaning of which they are capable, and the only meaning that they can have, that the test is whether an act is easy to operate; that is not the test of good legislation.
There is one point I must correct. He pointed out, with reference to my hon. friend from Essex East, that subclause (2) of clause 85 did not interfere with clause 18 of the bill. I cannot follow that argument at all. Clause 18 is a general clause giving a right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada over matters of law and jurisdiction. That applies to all orders under the board. But the minister, under paragraph 2 of clause 85 can exempt all companies from the operation

of this part of the bill. By doing that, he completely nullifies the bill in so far as those rights are concerned.
It seems to me that he has made no case at all and no cause that would justify the governor in council rendering inoperative this whole part of the bill which has to do with gas and power exports and imports. The effect of clause 85 (2), as it now stands, is that the governor in council can exempt all companies in Canada from the operation of the part. Surely that is not desirable or defensible legislation. I leave it on that simple ground and ask the minister to make some defence of that extraordinary request for arbitrary power that is quite out of keeping with any principle of legislation that I have ever heard asserted in this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: If the minister examines this language at all carefully, surely he will see that it would be perfectly competent for the governor in council-if parliament saw fit to accept this subsection (2); and may I say that when I have the minister's attention I shall be glad to continue-to exempt one pipe line and not another, or in other words, to have one come under the law and another not to come under the law. In other words, what the government is doing here is giving itself the power to make one law for one company and another law for another company. There is no limitation whatsoever upon the kind of company or the area or anything else that can be exempted. In other words, under this legislation you can at one fell swoop have a favoured instrument decided in secret in the cabinet, as was pointed out when the amendment was moved. Surely that is an entirely objectionable power to give to the cabinet. If they want to pick some special instrument and to clothe it with some special power and some special exemption, surely they could come to parliament and ask parliament to do that and disclose their reasons.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This part of the bill, Mr. Chairman, has to do with, among other things, the export and import of power or gas and also with the price that is charged therefor. The amendment now before us seeks to remove from the act the provision giving the authority to the governor in council by regulation to exempt any person or class of persons or any product or class of products from the provisions of this act.
I can very well recall how, only a limited number of years ago certain members of

this house did not want United States buccaneers, as they called them, to be instrumental in the building of the trans-Canada pipe line. Who did they initially have confidence in? It was an individual by the name of Mr. McMahon. They implored the Liberal government of the day please to invite Mr. McMahon and to see whether or not he would not be willing to build the trans-Canada pipe line.
We in the lower mainland of British Columbia have a "beef" against Mr. McMahon. Our complaint was investigated by the royal commission on energy. The royal commission had certain things to say with regard to the prices that were being charged to Canadian wholesalers of natural gas or Canadian distributors, prices in excess of those that were being charged to United States wholesalers south of the line. The Borden commission did not mince words in roundly and soundly condemning the practice of the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited.
Now we see what is happening with regard to this man who was a hero in the eyes of the Conservatives of this house only a limited number of years ago. We now see where this cabinet is asking for authority to exempt such an organization as Westcoast Transmission Company from any decision of the board that would have regard to the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him in relation to the public interest. We contend-and we have done so for a considerable length of time on the
Business of the House
lower mainland-that the public interest in British Columbia is not being served by the practice of Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. We were confirmed in our contention by the findings of the Borden commission, and now the government is asking us to authorize the company to continue these practices.
Progress reported.
